“Conspiracy game”

(A new chess variant)

Abstract

The classical game of chess is missing one of the most important aspects of a realistic combat between two armies – a secret traitor who would conspire against its own king.
In this study we are going to present a new chess variant that includes conspiracy and betrayal, and analyse all the implications that result from it.

Introduction

All the chess variants available to the public, regardless of their complexity, are missing the most important aspects that would make the game more realistic. Adding more pieces that move and behave differently, or even increasing the size of the chess board adds nothing to the overall strategy of the game. Not even arranging the same pieces randomly (see Bobby Fischer’s “Chess 960”) would solve this problem. We shall not confuse combinations and permutations with strategy.

A game of chess should not only represent entertainment, but education as well. A game of chess should educate people that not everybody plays fairly. A game of chess should educate people that in a realistic combat situation there are plenty of cheaters and opportunists, and plenty of room for betrayal.

Life is not fair. Neither the game of chess should be.

Mastering the rules should not be the only way to win a game. Rebellion and betrayal should be included as well.

Here comes our proposal.

Game layout

a) A chessboard of 10x10

b) Two players

c) Two colours: black and white in the first phase

d) A third colour, red, to represent rebels, in the second phase

e) Each player has 3 rows of pieces facing each other, the first row being the first line of attack, and so on.
The pieces

Each player has the following pieces:

a) 2 kings (a fake king and a real king)

b) 2 captains

c) 4 archers

d) 2 towers

e) 4 knights

f) 16 pawns (or soldiers)

Each army is divided into:

a) Infantry (pawns)

b) Cavalry (knights)

c) Officers (captains, archers and towers)

d) Royalty (the real king)

e) Traitors (the fake king)

The pieces are placed in the following way:

a) First row (10 pawns)

b) Second row (6 pawns in the middle and 2 knights on each side)

c) Third row (the two kings in the middle, and then on each side: 1 captain, 2 archers, 1 tower)

The rules

Rules will change depending on the two different phases of the game

Phase 1: Black king vs white king

a) The two kings have a sign underneath indicating which one is the real king, and which one is the fake king. They are placed randomly in the two central squares and only the player they belong to knows their true identity. Both of them move as in the classical chess game until the fake king decides or is forced to “betray” its own king.

b) The fake king is in fact the secret “treasurer” and it has the ability to betray its own king or to make opponent’s officers and knights switch side. It has the ability to move 4 squares in every direction, or to make 4 consecutive moves per turn (for a maximum of 4 squares).

c) The fake king becomes treasurer after the first move of revealing himself, and betraying his own king, forcing the king to play with his real identity

d) The treasurer does not capture pieces. Instead, if placed next to one of the opponent’s officers or knights, it makes them switch side. When captured, the treasurer will switch sides. When captured again, the treasurer will betray its new king. This time the treasurer will be removed from the chessboard. The opponent player will have to reveal his own real king, if not revealed yet.

e) The treasurer does not check the opponent’s king and can sit next to it without being captured by the king

f) At one turn the treasurer can corrupt more than one of the opponent’s officers and knights if passing or sitting next to them

g) Captains; move as the queen in the classical chess game

h) Archers; move as the bishop

i) Towers; move as the rook

j) Knights; move as the knight

k) Pawns; move as pawns and capture as pawns, with some differences. At every turn each player can move one pawn for one or two squares, or two pawns for one square each. In this case, only one pawn is allowed to capture. When reaching the opposite end of the chessboard a pawn might be promoted into a knight or officer that has been already captured, or into four pawns. If the player chooses to release four captured pawns, they are placed anywhere on the first two rows, on free squares (see above, the rows of pawns and knights).

l) Pawns will not betray their own king

m) An officer or knight who switched sides can switch sides once again

n) When a fake king reveals his identity as the treasurer, it takes a different shape. A special piece should exist for it.

o) An officer or knight sitting next to their own treasurer or king will not switch sides when under pressure from the opponent’s treasurer

p) When one treasurer comes next to one of the opponent’s kings (the fake and real king haven’t been revealed yet) they will have to reveal their identity.

q) In this case we have the following situations:

• if next to the fake king (or the treasurer) they might conspire to create the rebel army (see below)

• if next to the real king the treasurer will betray its own king and switch sides

Phase 2: Royals vs rebels

a) When one treasurer comes next to the opponents’ treasurer, they might form a rebel army and rebel against their own kings. The player who made this move takes charge of the rebel army, and the opponent takes charge of both remaining armies. A third colour, red, is introduced to represent the rebel army.

b) The player who decided to create the rebel army is allowed to take one extra turn with either an offensive or defensive move. From this point on each officer and knight who becomes corrupted will switch sides into the rebel army.

c) One turn is considered moving one treasurer 4 consecutive moves of 1 square each. The 4 moves can also be shared amongst the two rebel treasurers in order to corrupt more of the opponent’s pieces into switching sides

d) During one turn, it is not allowed to check one king more than once

e) It is not allowed to check both kings at the same time

f) In order to win, the rebel army has to exterminate both initial armies and to checkmate both kings

g) If one king is checkmated it becomes a prisoner which will be freed at the condition of creating one more treasurer by a “decree”. Its owner (the player who the royal army belongs to) is not allowed to move anything else until the checkmated king is released

h) Once a checkmated king is released, it is placed anywhere on the chessboard, on a safe place, accompanied by a new treasurer who belongs to the rebel army, has the colour of the rebel army, and is controlled by the player who controls the rebel army. The new treasurer is placed next to the king in a square where it could not be captured from the first move

i) The new treasurer is allowed to corrupt the royal army from within until it gets captured

j) If the two real kings come next to each other during the battle against the rebels, the player who controls this army is allowed (only once) to make one extra defensive move. A defensive move means that they do not directly attack any of the rebels.

k) The royal army can win even with only one king, if they exterminate the entire rebel army

l) If pawns get promoted during this phase, and if the player decides to promote them into releasing 4 pawns prisoners, they can be of any colour and could be placed around the king that needs more help, or shared amongst the two kings.

m) Pawns of different colours will no longer capture each other. Instead they will simply swap places if placed diagonally as in the classical capture mode for pawns

n) Pawns can also swap colour and join the king’s army that needs more help. Only two pawns at one turn are allowed to swap colour

o) Pawns will maintain their initial direction of moving corresponding to their colour. This direction will change after the colour swap

p) During the battle against rebels a treasurer might betray its new army again and switch sides if:

• Captured

• In impossibility to move (surrounded by pawns etc.)

• Coming next to one of the kings, or both

q) Black and white pieces will maintain their initial ability of checking or checkmating the other king. The player controlling them is not allowed to do so intentionally.

r) Black and white pieces will no longer capture each other. They will fight together against the rebel army

s) If one of the kings is accidentally checkmated, it is considered a victory for the rebels

Victory points

• If one king is checkmated in the first phase it is considered one victory

• In the second phase each winner gets two victory points, because there are two kings involved in the same army

Conclusion

This game requires some additional pieces, some additional rules and even a new army in reserve (to form the rebel army). Also the time required for a complete game might be a bit longer, but the experience acquired when dealing with conspiracy, betrayal and traitors is something new for a logical board game.
It is possible we might have missed out some important aspects of the game. That is because we have never made a simulation of this game. We have focused more on the idea of conspiracy, traitors and betrayal, and less on creating the final version of the rules that control this game. Rules could be changed, or improved, if it turns out that some of them are in conflict with the others. But the initial idea that most victorious battles in history are the product of conspiracy and betrayal shall not be changed.
